claim: Neuropilins are positive regulators of Hedgehog signaling.
source: Previous work has identified neuropilins, established semaphorin receptors, as positive regulators of Hedgehog signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work in the manuscript.

claim: Neuropilins require plexin co-receptors to mediate semaphorin signaling.
source: Neuropilins require plexin co-receptors to mediate semaphorin signaling, but the role of plexins in Hedgehog signaling has not yet been explored.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about semaphorin signaling.

claim: Multiple plexins promote Hedgehog signaling in NIH/3T3 mouse fibroblasts.
source: Here, we provide evidence that multiple plexins promote Hedgehog signaling in NIH/3T3 mouse fibroblasts and that plexin loss of function in these cells results in significantly reduced Hedgehog pathway activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including luciferase assays shown in Figure 1.

claim: Plexin loss of function in NIH/3T3 cells results in significantly reduced Hedgehog pathway activity.
source: Here, we provide evidence that multiple plexins promote Hedgehog signaling in NIH/3T3 mouse fibroblasts and that plexin loss of function in these cells results in significantly reduced Hedgehog pathway activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from siRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 1H and I.

claim: Catalytic activity of the plexin GTPase-activating protein (GAP) domain is required for Hedgehog signal promotion.
source: Catalytic activity of the plexin GTPase-activating protein (GAP) domain is required for Hedgehog signal promotion, and constitutive activation of the GAP domain further amplifies Hedgehog signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from GAP domain mutant constructs shown in Figure 3.

claim: Constitutive activation of the plexin GAP domain further amplifies Hedgehog signaling.
source: Catalytic activity of the plexin GTPase-activating protein (GAP) domain is required for Hedgehog signal promotion, and constitutive activation of the GAP domain further amplifies Hedgehog signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from PLXNA1ΔECD constructs shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Plexins promote Hedgehog signaling at the level of GLI transcription factors.
source: Additionally, we demonstrate that plexins promote Hedgehog signaling at the level of GLI transcription factors and that this promotion requires intact primary cilia.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from SmoM2 and Gli1 co-transfection experiments shown in Figure 3O and P.

claim: Plexin-mediated promotion of Hedgehog signaling requires intact primary cilia.
source: Additionally, we demonstrate that plexins promote Hedgehog signaling at the level of GLI transcription factors and that this promotion requires intact primary cilia.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Kif3a-/- NIH/3T3 cells shown in Figure 4O and P.

claim: Plexin loss of function significantly reduces the response to Hedgehog pathway activation in the mouse dentate gyrus.
source: Finally, we find that plexin loss of function significantly reduces the response to Hedgehog pathway activation in the mouse dentate gyrus.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Plxna1-/- and Plxna2-/- mice shown in Figure 7.

claim: PTCH1 inhibits pathway activity by repressing Smoothened (SMO) in the absence of HH ligand.
source: In the absence of HH ligand, the 12-pass transmembrane (TM) protein Patched 1 (PTCH1) inhibits pathway activity by repressing a second cell-surface protein Smoothened (SMO), a 7-pass TM protein with GPCR-like activity (Alcedo et al., 1996; Marigo and Tabin, 1996; Stone et al., 1996; van den Heuvel and Ingham, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: HH ligand binding to PTCH1 leads to de-repression of SMO.
source: HH ligand binding to PTCH1 leads to de-repression of SMO, which shifts the processing of GLI transcription factors from repressor to activator forms, thus altering the balance of HH target gene expression (Hui and Angers, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: De-repression of SMO shifts the processing of GLI transcription factors from repressor to activator forms.
source: HH ligand binding to PTCH1 leads to de-repression of SMO, which shifts the processing of GLI transcription factors from repressor to activator forms, thus altering the balance of HH target gene expression (Hui and Angers, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: HH signaling directs embryonic and postnatal development as well as adult tissue homeostasis.
source: By balancing the activity of these key molecules, HH signaling directs embryonic and postnatal development as well as adult tissue homeostasis in a wide variety of cellular contexts.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: HH pathway disruption can drive cancer.
source: In contrast, HH pathway disruption can drive a number of diseases, including cancer (Teglund and Toftgård, 2010; Briscoe and Thérond, 2013; Petrova and Joyner, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Many cell surface regulators of HH signaling have partially redundant functions.
source: Notably, many of these cell surface regulators have partially redundant functions (Zhang et al., 2001; Jeong and McMahon, 2005; Allen et al., 2007; Allen et al., 2011; Izzi et al., 2011; Holtz et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Vertebrate HH signaling requires the primary cilium.
source: Further, increased complexity within vertebrate HH signaling, including a requirement for the primary cilium, has made it difficult to study HH regulators that lack invertebrate counterparts, such as Scube2 and GAS1 (Ingham et al., 2011; Wierbowski et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Neuropilins directly interact with class 3 SEMA ligands.
source: Neuropilins (NRPs) directly interact with class 3 SEMA ligands and require plexin (PLXN) co-receptors to transduce SEMA signals intracellularly (Chen et al., 1997; He and Tessier-Lavigne, 1997; Kolodkin et al., 1997; Takahashi et al., 1999; Tamagnone et al., 1999; Gu et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Membrane-bound SEMA and Sema3E interact directly with PLXN extracellular domains.
source: Membrane-bound SEMA and Sema3E interact directly with PLXN extracellular domains (ECDs) to activate downstream signaling events, which lead to remodeling and disassembly of the cytoskeleton (Barberis et al., 2004; Neufeld and Kessler, 2008; Jongbloets and Pasterkamp, 2014; Rich et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: PLXNs are a family of conserved, single-pass TM proteins containing nine different receptor types.
source: PLXNs are a family of conserved, single-pass TM proteins containing nine different receptor types, which fall into four subfamilies based on homology (A, B, C, and D) (Tamagnone et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The cytoplasmic domain of all PLXN family members harbors a GTPase-activating protein (GAP) domain.
source: The cytoplasmic domain (CD) of all PLXN family members harbors a GTPase-activating protein (GAP) domain (Rohm et al., 2000b; Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Catalytic activity of the PLXN GAP domain is necessary for SEMA-mediated cytoskeletal remodeling and cell migration.
source: Catalytic activity of the PLXN GAP domain is necessary for SEMA-mediated cytoskeletal remodeling and cell migration (Hota and Buck, 2012; Wang et al., 2013; Zhao et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: NRPs positively regulate HH signaling through their cytoplasmic domains.
source: Multiple lines of evidence show that NRPs positively regulate HH signaling through their CDs (Ge et al., 2015; Hillman et al., 2011; Pinskey et al., 2017); however, the role of PLXNs in HH signaling remains unexplored.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Plxna1 expression significantly increases HH pathway activation compared to a vector-transfected control.
source: Strikingly, and similar to what we previously observed with Nrp1 (Pinskey et al., 2017), Plxna1 expression significantly increases HH pathway activation compared to a vector-transfected (pCIG) control (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: PLXNA1 does not promote HH signaling in the absence of pathway activation with HH ligand.
source: Of note, PLXNA1 does not promote HH signaling in the absence of pathway activation with HH ligand (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: All members of the PLXN A subfamily promote HH signaling following pathway activation with HH ligand.
source: Our data suggest that all members of the PLXN A subfamily promote HH signaling following pathway activation with HH ligand (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-E.

claim: PLXNB2 promotes HH signaling to a similar extent as PLXNs from the A subfamily.
source: Surprisingly, PLXNB2 also promotes HH signaling to a similar extent as PLXNs from the A subfamily, suggesting that PLXN-mediated HH promotion may be independent of NRP interaction (Figure 1F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F and G.

claim: PLXN-mediated HH promotion may be independent of NRP interaction.
source: Surprisingly, PLXNB2 also promotes HH signaling to a similar extent as PLXNs from the A subfamily, suggesting that PLXN-mediated HH promotion may be independent of NRP interaction (Figure 1F and G).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that PLXNB2, which is not known to interact with NRPs, promotes HH signaling.

claim: GFRα1 does not promote HH signaling.
source: Importantly, GFRα1, an unrelated cell-surface protein within the glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor receptor (GFR) family, does not promote HH signaling (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: NIH/3T3 cells express Plxna1 and Plxnb2 most highly, followed by Plxnd1, Plxna3, and Plxna2.
source: According to RNA-sequencing data from the ENCODE project (ENCODE Project Consortium, 2012; Davis et al., 2018), NIH/3T3 fibroblasts express a subset of Plxns at varying levels, with Plxna1 and Plxnb2 most highly expressed, followed by Plxnd1, Plxna3, and Plxna2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data from the ENCODE project shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Plxna1-/-;Plxna2-/- MEFs still respond to SAG activation of HH signaling.
source: Interestingly, both cell lines lacking Plxna1 and Plxna2 still respond to SAG activation of HH signaling, as measured by expression of the direct HH transcriptional targets, Gli1 and Ptch1 (Figure 1H and I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H and I.

claim: Plxna1-/-;Plxna2-/- cells treated with Plxn siRNAs responded significantly less to SAG activation of Gli1 and Ptch1 compared to BLOCK-iT controls.
source: Strikingly, both cell lines treated with the Plxn siRNAs listed above responded significantly less to SAG activation of Gli1 and Ptch1 compared to BLOCK-iT controls (Figure 1H and I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H and I.

claim: The degree of reduction following Plxn depletion is similar to that observed with Nrp depletion.
source: The degree of reduction following Plxn depletion is similar to that observed with Nrp depletion using previously published siRNA reagents targeting Nrp1 and Nrp2 (Hillman et al., 2011; Figure 1H and I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H and I.

claim: Deleting the PLXNA1 TM and CD abrogates PLXNA1-mediated promotion of HH signaling in NIH/3T3 cells.
source: Interestingly, deleting the PLXNA1 TM and CD (PLXNA1ΔTMCD) or the CD alone (PLXNA1ΔCD) abrogates PXLNA1-mediated promotion of HH signaling in NIH/3T3 cells (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Deleting the PLXNA1 CD alone abrogates PLXNA1-mediated promotion of HH signaling in NIH/3T3 cells.
source: Interestingly, deleting the PLXNA1 TM and CD (PLXNA1ΔTMCD) or the CD alone (PLXNA1ΔCD) abrogates PXLNA1-mediated promotion of HH signaling in NIH/3T3 cells (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: PLXNA1ΔTMCD is secreted.
source: Western blot analyses confirmed PLXNA1, PLXNA1ΔTMCD, and PLXNA1ΔCD expression and PLXNA1ΔTMCD secretion (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: PLXNA1 and PLXNA1ΔCD localize to the cell surface.
source: Further, immunofluorescence staining for an extracellular MYC epitope under permeabilizing and non-permeabilizing conditions confirmed the cell surface localization of PLXNA1 and PLXNA1ΔCD as well as the secretion of PLXNA1ΔTMCD compared to a control BOC construct with a C-terminal MYC tag (Figure 2D–K).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2D-K.

claim: PLXNA1ΔECD is still able to promote HH signaling.
source: Not only is PLXNA1ΔECD still able to promote HH signaling, but the constitutively active PLXN GAP domain significantly augments the level of HH promotion (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The constitutively active PLXN GAP domain significantly augments the level of HH promotion.
source: Not only is PLXNA1ΔECD still able to promote HH signaling, but the constitutively active PLXN GAP domain significantly augments the level of HH promotion (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Full-length PLXN boosts HH signaling one and a half- to twofold on average.
source: While full-length PLXN boosts HH signaling one and a half- to twofold on average, PLXNA1ΔECD consistently increases the level of HH signaling between four- and tenfold, averaging an approximately sixfold increase (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: PLXNA1ΔECD consistently increases the level of HH signaling between four- and tenfold, averaging an approximately sixfold increase.
source: While full-length PLXN boosts HH signaling one and a half- to twofold on average, PLXNA1ΔECD consistently increases the level of HH signaling between four- and tenfold, averaging an approximately sixfold increase (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Arginine to alanine mutations in residues 1429 and 1430 of mouse PLXNA1 disrupt GAP activity.
source: Arginine to alanine mutations in residues 1429 and 1430 of mouse PLXNA1 disrupt GAP activity, rendering PLXNA1 a nonfunctional SEMA receptor in a COS7 cell collapse assay (Rohm et al., 2000a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Arginine mutations within the PLXNA1 GAP domain render PLXNA1 unable to promote HH signaling.
source: Strikingly, recapitulating these conserved arginine mutations within the PLXNA1 GAP domain also rendered PLXNA1 unable to promote HH signaling (PLXNA1R1; Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Analogous mutations in PLXNB2 abrogate the promotion of HH pathway activity.
source: Importantly, analogous mutations in PLXNB2 also abrogate the promotion of HH pathway activity (PLXNB2R1; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: The A1R1 arginine to alanine GAP mutations in the context of the PLXNA1 ECD deletion significantly reduce the level of HH promotion.
source: Further, the A1R1 arginine to alanine GAP mutations in the context of the PLXNA1 ECD deletion significantly reduce the level of HH promotion, though they do not completely abrogate PLXN-mediated HH pathway induction when compared with PLXNA1ΔCD (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Other cytoplasmic determinants contribute to PLXN-mediated HH promotion.
source: These data suggest that other cytoplasmic determinants contribute to PLXN-mediated HH promotion.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that GAP mutations do not completely abrogate HH promotion.

claim: Mutation of a second tyrosine residue (PLXNA1Y2ΔECD) abrogated promotion of HH signaling to comparable levels to the A1R1 mutation.
source: While mutation of one tyrosine residue alone (PLXNA1Y1ΔECD) or in conjunction with the A1R1 mutation (PLXNA1R1Y1ΔECD) did not impact PLXN function (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C), mutation of a second tyrosine residue (PLXNA1Y2ΔECD) abrogated promotion of HH signaling to comparable levels to the A1R1 mutation (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Mutation of both the GAP domain and the second FYN kinase phosphorylation site (PLXNA1R1Y2∆ECD) rendered PLXN completely inert in the context of HH signal transduction.
source: Notably, mutation of both the GAP domain and the second FYN kinase phosphorylation site (PLXNA1R1Y2∆ECD) rendered PLXN completely inert (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C) in the context of HH signal transduction.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: GAP activity and FYN kinase phosphorylation are necessary for PLXN-mediated promotion of HH signaling.
source: Together, these results suggest that GAP activity and FYN kinase phosphorylation are necessary for PLXN-mediated promotion of HH signaling.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data on GAP and FYN kinase mutations.

claim: PLXNA1 does not promote Wnt pathway activation.
source: Whereas either β-CATENIN expression or Chiron treatment significantly activates Wnt signaling in NIH/3T3 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B and C), PLXNA1 does not promote Wnt pathway activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B and C.

claim: PLXNA1 inhibits Wnt pathway activity.
source: Instead, PLXNA1, and to a greater degree PLXNA1ΔECD, inhibit Wnt pathway activity, with PLXNA1ΔECD reducing Wnt pathway activity to baseline levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B and C.

claim: PLXN does not act to generally promote transcription.
source: These data suggest that PLXN does not act to generally promote transcription, and instead has opposing consequences on HH and Wnt transcriptional readouts.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that PLXN promotes HH but inhibits Wnt signaling.

claim: Co-transfection of SmoM2 or Gli1 with a GAP-deficient Plxn (Plxna1r1ΔECD) returns HH pathway activation to near-baseline levels.
source: Notably, this promotion requires GAP activity as co-transfection of SmoM2 or Gli1 with a GAP-deficient Plxn (Plxna1r1ΔECD) returns HH pathway activation to near-baseline levels (Figure 3O and P).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3O and P.

claim: PLXNs function downstream of HH ligand at the level of GLI or transcriptional regulation.
source: These data suggest that PLXNs function downstream of HH ligand at the level of GLI or transcriptional regulation, and that full PLXN GAP activation via the release of extracellular autoinhibition is necessary for enhanced HH promotion beyond the level observed with either SmoM2 or Gli1 alone.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data on SmoM2 and Gli1 co-transfection.

claim: Full PLXN GAP activation via the release of extracellular autoinhibition is necessary for enhanced HH promotion beyond the level observed with either SmoM2 or Gli1 alone.
source: These data suggest that PLXNs function downstream of HH ligand at the level of GLI or transcriptional regulation, and that full PLXN GAP activation via the release of extracellular autoinhibition is necessary for enhanced HH promotion beyond the level observed with either SmoM2 or Gli1 alone.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data on PLXNA1ΔECD.

claim: The primary cilium is an important platform for HH signaling molecules.
source: The primary cilium is an important platform for HH signaling molecules (Wong et al., 2009; Goetz and Anderson, 2010) and many HH pathway components, including NRP, are enriched there (Corbit et al., 2005; Haycraft et al., 2005; Rohatgi et al., 2007; Pinskey et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Many HH pathway components, including NRP, are enriched in the primary cilium.
source: The primary cilium is an important platform for HH signaling molecules (Wong et al., 2009; Goetz and Anderson, 2010) and many HH pathway components, including NRP, are enriched there (Corbit et al., 2005; Haycraft et al., 2005; Rohatgi et al., 2007; Pinskey et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Molecules over 40 kDa are unable to freely diffuse into the primary cilium.
source: Notably, molecules over 40 kDa are unable to freely diffuse into the primary cilium, requiring active transport to enter this highly regulated subcellular compartment (Kee et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: PLXN staining was not enriched within the primary cilium for any of the constructs tested.
source: Unlike NRP1, PLXN staining was not enriched within the primary cilium for any of the constructs we tested (Figure 4A–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A-G.

claim: PLXNs do not accumulate in the primary cilium even in Dync2h1lln/lln MEFs.
source: However, even in Dync2h1lln/lln MEFs, PLXNs still do not accumulate in the primary cilium (Figure 4H–N).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4H-N.

claim: PLXN localization to primary cilia is not required to regulate HH signal transduction.
source: These data suggest that PLXN localization to primary cilia is not required to regulate HH signal transduction.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that PLXNs do not localize to primary cilia but still regulate HH signaling.

claim: Kif3a-/- NIH/3T3 cells do not respond to SmoM2 transfection.
source: As expected, WT NIH/3T3 cells activate HH signaling in response to SmoM2 transfection, while Kif3a-/- NIH/3T3 cells do not (Figure 4O).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4O.

claim: Kif3a-/- NIH/3T3 cells do not respond to co-transfection with SmoM2 and Plxna1∆ECD.
source: Notably, Kif3a-/- NIH/3T3 cells also do not respond to co-transfection with SmoM2 and Plxna1∆ECD (Figure 4O).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4O.

claim: GLI1 and GLI2ΔN promote HH pathway activation in the absence of primary cilia.
source: Both GLI1 and GLI2ΔN have been reported to promote HH pathway activation in the absence of primary cilia (Haycraft et al., 2005; Wong et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Co-transfecting Kif3a-/- NIH/3T3 cells with either Gli1 or Gli2∆N and Plxna1∆ECD displayed no further promotion of HH signaling.
source: Strikingly, and distinct from what we observe in WT NIH/3T3 cells, co-transfecting Kif3a-/- NIH/3T3 cells with either Gli1 or Gli2∆N and Plxna1∆ECD displayed no further promotion of HH signaling (Figure 4P; Figure 3P).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4P.

claim: Primary cilia are required for PLXN-dependent promotion of HH signaling.
source: These data suggest that, while PLXNs do not localize to the primary cilium, primary cilia are required for PLXN-dependent promotion of HH signaling.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data in Kif3a-/- cells.

claim: Plxna1 transfection does not affect SMO localization to primary cilia.
source: Further, Plxna1 transfection does not affect SMO localization to primary cilia, ciliary length, or the rate of ciliation amongst cells after treatment with HH-conditioned media or control-conditioned media (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-G.

claim: Plxna1 transfection does not affect ciliary length.
source: Further, Plxna1 transfection does not affect SMO localization to primary cilia, ciliary length, or the rate of ciliation amongst cells after treatment with HH-conditioned media or control-conditioned media (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-G.

claim: Plxna1 transfection does not affect the rate of ciliation amongst cells.
source: Further, Plxna1 transfection does not affect SMO localization to primary cilia, ciliary length, or the rate of ciliation amongst cells after treatment with HH-conditioned media or control-conditioned media (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-G.

claim: No difference was observed in vivo in ciliary length or ciliation frequency in the dentate gyrus of Plxna2-/- mice compared to heterozygous littermates.
source: Importantly, no difference was observed in vivo in ciliary length or ciliation frequency in the dentate gyrus of Plxna2-/- mice compared to heterozygous littermates (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H and I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1H and I.

claim: SHH is initially secreted from the notochord.
source: SHH, which is initially secreted from the notochord, signals in a ventral–dorsal gradient to specify distinct cell fates in the neural tube.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: SHH signals in a ventral–dorsal gradient to specify distinct cell fates in the neural tube.
source: SHH, which is initially secreted from the notochord, signals in a ventral–dorsal gradient to specify distinct cell fates in the neural tube.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: SHH controls cell proliferation and cell migration in the neural tube.
source: Notably, SHH also controls cell proliferation and cell migration in this tissue (Cayuso and Martí, 2005; Cayuso et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Multiple Plxns are expressed in the developing chicken neural tube concomitant with SHH-dependent tissue patterning.
source: Previous work demonstrated that multiple Plxns are expressed in the developing chicken neural tube concomitant with SHH-dependent tissue patterning (Mauti et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Electroporation with an empty vector (pCIG) does not impact neural tube patterning.
source: While electroporation with an empty vector (pCIG) does not impact neural tube patterning (Figure 5A–D), SmoM2 electroporation drives ectopic expression of NKX6.1, a direct target of HH signaling that is normally restricted ventrally, in the dorsal neural tube (Figure 5E–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A-D.

claim: SmoM2 electroporation drives ectopic expression of NKX6.1 in the dorsal neural tube.
source: While electroporation with an empty vector (pCIG) does not impact neural tube patterning (Figure 5A–D), SmoM2 electroporation drives ectopic expression of NKX6.1, a direct target of HH signaling that is normally restricted ventrally, in the dorsal neural tube (Figure 5E–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E-H.

claim: Gli1 electroporation results in expansion of the NKX6.1 domain.
source: Similarly, electroporation with Gli1, an obligate activator of the HH pathway that drives high levels of HH signaling, also results in expansion of the NKX6.1 domain (Figure 5I–L).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5I-L.

claim: Quantitation of the NKX6.1 domain size revealed no significant differences between pCIG- and Plxna1∆ECD-electroporated embryos.
source: In some Plxna1∆ECD-electroporated embryos, we observed apparent ectopic NKX6.1 expression (Figure 5P, Figure 5—figure supplement 1K, yellow arrowheads); however, quantitation of the NKX6.1 domain size revealed no significant differences between pCIG- and Plxna1∆ECD-electroporated embryos (Figure 5—figure supplement 1J–M).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1J-M.

claim: Electroporation of Plxna1∆ECD phenocopies Gli1-induced migration into the lumen of the neural tube.
source: Gli1 expression also results in ectopic migration of cells into the dorsal lumen of the neural tube, which is typically completely devoid of cells (Figure 5I, yellow asterisk). Electroporation of Plxna1∆ECD phenocopies Gli1-induced migration into the lumen of the neural tube (Figure 5M–P, yellow asterisk), with a similar loss of PAX7-positive cells on the electroporated side (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5M-P.

claim: PLXN-dependent ectopic cell migration is lost upon mutation of the intracellular PLXN GAP domain.
source: Importantly, PLXN-dependent ectopic cell migration is lost upon mutation of the intracellular PLXN GAP domain (Figure 5Q–T, white asterisk).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5Q-T.

claim: Ptch1∆L2 expression inhibits endogenous HH pathway activity.
source: Consistent with previous reports, Ptch1∆L2 expression inhibits endogenous HH pathway activity, visualized by the cell-autonomous loss of NKX6.1 in electroporated cells in the ventral neural tube (Figure 6F–J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F-J and citations to previous reports.

claim: Cells co-electroporated with Ptch1∆L2 and Plxna1∆ECD no longer migrate.
source: Whereas cell migration is observed in the dorsal lumen of Plxna1∆ECD-electroporated neural tubes (Figure 6K–O, yellow asterisk), cells co-electroporated with Ptch1∆L2 and Plxna1∆ECD no longer migrate (Figure 6P–T).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6P-T.

claim: Increased PLXN-mediated migration in the neural tube is HH-dependent.
source: These data suggest that increased PLXN-mediated migration in the neural tube is HH-dependent.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that Ptch1∆L2 blocks PLXN-mediated migration.

claim: Neuronal progenitor cells in the hippocampus rely on HH signaling for proliferation and maintenance, particularly within the dentate gyrus.
source: Interestingly, developing neurons and progenitor cells in the hippocampus express Plxns (Cheng et al., 2001) and neuronal progenitor cells rely on HH signaling for proliferation and maintenance, particularly within the dentate gyrus (Machold et al., 2003; Ahn and Joyner, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Plxna1-/- mice have significantly fewer Gli1-positive cells in both the dorsal and ventral dentate gyrus compared to their heterozygous littermates.
source: Plxna1-/- mice have significantly fewer Gli1-positive cells in both the dorsal and ventral dentate gyrus compared to their heterozygous littermates (Figure 7A–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A-F.

claim: Plxna2 deletion has a similar effect on Gli1 expression with significantly fewer β-galactosidase-positive cells detected in the hilus and subgranular zone of the dorsal and ventral dentate gyrus.
source: Plxna2 deletion has a similar effect on Gli1 expression with significantly fewer β-galactosidase-positive cells detected in the hilus and subgranular zone of the dorsal and ventral dentate gyrus (Figure 7G–L).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7G-L.

claim: No differences were observed in BrdU+ or TUNEL+ cells in Plxna1-/- or Plxna2-/- mice compared to heterozygous littermates.
source: Further, no differences were observed in BrdU+ or TUNEL+ cells in Plxna1-/- or Plxna2-/- mice compared to heterozygous littermates, indicating that Plxna1 or Plxna2 deletion does not significantly impact cell proliferation or cell death, respectively (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–L, Figure 7—figure supplement 2A–L).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-L and Figure 7—figure supplement 2A-L.

claim: Plxna1 or Plxna2 deletion does not significantly impact cell proliferation or cell death.
source: Further, no differences were observed in BrdU+ or TUNEL+ cells in Plxna1-/- or Plxna2-/- mice compared to heterozygous littermates, indicating that Plxna1 or Plxna2 deletion does not significantly impact cell proliferation or cell death, respectively (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–L, Figure 7—figure supplement 2A–L).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the BrdU and TUNEL staining data.

claim: Plxna1-/-; Plxna2-/- embryos die prenatally.
source: Unfortunately, Plxna1-/-; Plxna2-/- embryos die prenatally, precluding analyses of any potential additive or synergistic effects on HH pathway activity in the postnatal dentate gyrus.
evidence: This claim is based on observations from mouse breeding experiments.

claim: PLXNs regulate HH pathway activation in vivo.
source: Together, these data suggest that PLXNs regulate HH pathway activation in vivo and suggest that multiple PLXNs regulate HH signaling in the developing mouse hippocampus.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the in vivo data in the dentate gyrus.

claim: Multiple PLXNs regulate HH signaling in the developing mouse hippocampus.
source: Together, these data suggest that PLXNs regulate HH pathway activation in vivo and suggest that multiple PLXNs regulate HH signaling in the developing mouse hippocampus.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that both Plxna1 and Plxna2 deletion affect HH signaling in the hippocampus.

claim: The mechanism of NRP action in HH signaling may diverge from its mechanism in SEMA signaling.
source: Interestingly, while the mechanism of NRP action in HH signaling may diverge from its mechanism in SEMA signaling (Andreyeva et al., 2011; Ge et al., 2015; Pinskey et al., 2017), we discover that PLXNs function similarly in SEMA and HH cascades.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: PLXNs function similarly in SEMA and HH cascades.
source: Interestingly, while the mechanism of NRP action in HH signaling may diverge from its mechanism in SEMA signaling (Andreyeva et al., 2011; Ge et al., 2015; Pinskey et al., 2017), we discover that PLXNs function similarly in SEMA and HH cascades.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that GAP activity is required for both SEMA and HH signaling.

claim: Deleting the PLXN ECD to create a constitutively active receptor augments HH promotion.
source: Further, deleting the PLXN ECD to create a constitutively active receptor augments HH promotion and alters HH-dependent tissue patterning and cell migration in the embryonic chicken neural tube, suggesting that PLXNs positively regulate HH signaling through GAP enzymatic activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from chicken neural tube electroporation experiments.

claim: Deleting the PLXN ECD alters HH-dependent tissue patterning and cell migration in the embryonic chicken neural tube.
source: Further, deleting the PLXN ECD to create a constitutively active receptor augments HH promotion and alters HH-dependent tissue patterning and cell migration in the embryonic chicken neural tube, suggesting that PLXNs positively regulate HH signaling through GAP enzymatic activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from chicken neural tube electroporation experiments shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: PLXNs positively regulate HH signaling through GAP enzymatic activity.
source: Further, deleting the PLXN ECD to create a constitutively active receptor augments HH promotion and alters HH-dependent tissue patterning and cell migration in the embryonic chicken neural tube, suggesting that PLXNs positively regulate HH signaling through GAP enzymatic activity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data on GAP domain mutations and ECD deletions.

claim: NRPs and PLXNs are expressed in a wide variety of tissues during active HH regulation.
source: Canonical SEMA receptors, the NRPs and PLXNs, are expressed in a wide variety of tissues during active HH regulation (Kawasaki et al., 1999; Perälä et al., 2005; Mauti et al., 2006; Perälä et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Unlike many previously described cell surface HH regulators, which interact directly with HH ligands, PLXNs promote HH signaling through their CDs at the level of GLI regulation.
source: Unlike many previously described cell surface HH regulators, which interact directly with HH ligands, PLXNs promote HH signaling through their CDs at the level of GLI regulation (Figure 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The PLXN GAP domain is important for canonical SEMA signaling as well as amplification of HH signaling.
source: This shows that the PLXN GAP domain is important for canonical SEMA signaling as well as amplification of HH signaling.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data on GAP domain function.

claim: NRPs and PLXNs function within other signaling pathways beyond SEMA signaling.
source: While NRPs and PLXNs were first described as SEMA receptors, they also function within other signaling pathways (He and Tessier-Lavigne, 1997; Kolodkin et al., 1997; Takahashi et al., 1999; Tamagnone et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: NRPs play roles in VEGF signaling to regulate angiogenesis.
source: NRPs play roles in VEGF signaling to regulate angiogenesis, and they interact with a wide variety of proteins, including PIGF-2, heparan sulfate, TGF-β1, HGF, PDGF, FGF, L1-CAM, integrins, and SARS-CoV-2 spike protein (Roth et al., 2008; Prud'homme and Glinka, 2012; Muhl et al., 2017; Sarabipour and Mac Gabhann, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: PLXNs form complexes with off-track, MET, Ron, scatter factor, Ig-CAMs, and VEGFR2 under various cellular conditions.
source: PLXNs also form complexes with off-track, MET, Ron, scatter factor, Ig-CAMs, and VEGFR2 under various cellular conditions (Winberg et al., 2001; Giordano et al., 2002; Conrotto et al., 2004; Toyofuku et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Altered SEMA/PLXN signaling is linked to cancer.
source: Multiple lines of evidence link altered SEMA/PLXN signaling to cancer. Depending on context, aberrant SEMA signaling may promote or suppress tumor growth and lead to various types of cancer (Neufeld et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: A link between altered PLXN signaling and increased HH signaling is intriguing because of the well-established role of elevated HH signaling in malignancies.
source: A link to increased HH signaling is intriguing because of the well-established role of elevated HH signaling in malignancies.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge and speculation about the implications of the findings.

claim: Addition of SEMA ligands in combination with HH ligand or SAG increased HH signaling in NIH/3T3 cells.
source: In one study, addition of SEMA ligands in combination with HH ligand or SAG increased HH signaling in NIH/3T3 cells (Ge et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Blocking NRP interaction with SEMA ligand reduces GLI expression.
source: Conversely, blocking NRP interaction with SEMA ligand reduces GLI expression (Ge et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Addition of SEMA ligand has no effect on HH signaling.
source: However, other studies suggest that addition of SEMA ligand has no effect on HH signaling (Hillman et al., 2011), and that NRPs still promote HH signaling when co-transfected with a version of GLI2 that cannot be phosphorylated by PKA at seven important sites (Pinskey et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: NRPs still promote HH signaling when co-transfected with a version of GLI2 that cannot be phosphorylated by PKA at seven important sites.
source: However, other studies suggest that addition of SEMA ligand has no effect on HH signaling (Hillman et al., 2011), and that NRPs still promote HH signaling when co-transfected with a version of GLI2 that cannot be phosphorylated by PKA at seven important sites (Pinskey et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: NIH/3T3 cells express endogenous PLXNs.
source: It is important to consider that NIH/3T3 cells, in which these studies were performed, express endogenous PLXNs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: SEMA ligands may act through endogenous PLXNs to increase HH reporter activity by stimulating GAP activity.
source: Given the results presented here, an alternate explanation of SEMA-mediated HH promotion is that SEMA ligands act through endogenous PLXNs to increase HH reporter activity by stimulating GAP activity.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the findings of the current study.

claim: PLXNs themselves or PLXN-NRP complexes may recruit PDE4D to the cell membrane rather than NRPs alone.
source: It is also possible that PLXNs themselves or PLXN-NRP complexes recruit PDE4D to the cell membrane rather than NRPs alone.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing an alternative mechanism.

claim: NRPs promote HH signaling through a novel cytoplasmic motif.
source: We previously reported that NRPs promote HH signaling through a novel cytoplasmic motif (Pinskey et al., 2017), within a region of the protein that is dispensable for SEMA signaling (Fantin et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The NRP cytoplasmic motif that promotes HH signaling is within a region of the protein that is dispensable for SEMA signaling.
source: We previously reported that NRPs promote HH signaling through a novel cytoplasmic motif (Pinskey et al., 2017), within a region of the protein that is dispensable for SEMA signaling (Fantin et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Deleting the NRP ECD does not disrupt HH pathway promotion.
source: First, deleting the NRP ECD, which mediates interaction between NRPs, PLXNs, and SEMA ligands, does not disrupt HH pathway promotion (Pinskey et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: PLXNB2 can promote HH signaling, despite its lack of reported interactions with NRPs.
source: Furthermore, we report here that PLXNB2 can promote HH signaling, despite its lack of reported interactions with NRPs (Neufeld and Kessler, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F and G.

claim: The PLXN CD interacts with a plethora of intracellular proteins.
source: The PLXN CD interacts with a plethora of intracellular proteins, including collapse-response-mediator protein (CRMP) family phosphoproteins, protein kinases, MICAL redox proteins, and small intracellular GTPases from the Rho, Ras, and Rap superfamilies (Püschel, 2007; Yang and Terman, 2013; Jongbloets and Pasterkamp, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Our understanding of the cellular mechanisms downstream of the PLXN GAP domain remains incomplete.
source: Further, our understanding of the cellular mechanisms downstream of the PLXN GAP domain remains incomplete, including which GTPases are regulated by various PLXN family members.
evidence: This claim is based on the current state of scientific knowledge.

claim: PLXNs from both the A and B subfamilies can promote HH signaling.
source: Here, we find that PLXNs from both the A and B subfamilies can promote HH signaling, which may be an important clue in answering this question.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: PLXNs likely converge upon a common protein or set of proteins that mediate HH promotion.
source: While we cannot exclude the possibility that each PLXN or PLXN subfamily regulates HH differently, it is likely that they converge upon a common protein or set of proteins that mediate HH promotion.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the observation that multiple PLXNs promote HH signaling.

claim: The PLXN family of proteins is comprised of nine members with distinct and overlapping functions.
source: As previously discussed, the PLXN family of proteins is comprised of nine members with distinct and overlapping functions (Neufeld and Kessler, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: One shared feature between all PLXN proteins is the conserved cytoplasmic GAP domain.
source: One shared feature between all PLXN proteins is the conserved cytoplasmic GAP domain (Neufeld and Kessler, 2008), which we find mediates HH signal promotion.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work and experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: PLXNs exhibit largely overlapping expression patterns in vivo.
source: It is also important to consider that PLXNs exhibit largely overlapping expression patterns in vivo, further complicating loss-of-function studies (Perälä et al., 2005; Mauti et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Deleting Plxna1 or Plxna2 alone is sufficient to reduce HH target gene expression in the dentate gyrus.
source: Notably, our results suggest that deleting Plxna1 or Plxna2 alone is sufficient to reduce HH target gene expression in the dentate gyrus (Figure 7), despite the widespread expression of additional Plxns in the central nervous system (Perälä et al., 2005), including Plxna3, which is highly expressed in the developing hippocampus (Cheng et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.
